reference.source: Textbook of Pediatric Rheumatology / ILAR & PRINTO criteria
clinicalPearls: Defined as arthritis affecting five or more joints within the first six months, and divided by the ILAR system into rheumatoid-factor-positive and rheumatoid-factor-negative subtypes

The rheumatoid-factor-positive form resembles adult seropositive rheumatoid arthritis, typically in older girls, with symmetrical small-joint involvement and a higher risk of erosions and rheumatoid nodules
Anti-citrullinated peptide antibodies often accompany rheumatoid-factor positivity and reinforce a more aggressive, erosive phenotype
The rheumatoid-factor-negative form is more heterogeneous, may present at any age and can involve large and small joints
Cervical spine and temporomandibular joint involvement can cause neck stiffness, micrognathia and feeding or airway difficulties
Chronic anterior uveitis is less frequent than in oligoarticular disease but still warrants slit-lamp surveillance, particularly in antinuclear-antibody-positive children
Early disease-modifying therapy with methotrexate, escalating to TNF inhibition or other biologics, aims to prevent joint destruction
reference.pathophysiology: Polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis is a chronic autoimmune synovitis in which activated T cells, B cells and proinflammatory cytokines including tumour necrosis factor drive proliferative synovial inflammation. The inflamed synovium forms a pannus that invades and erodes cartilage and subchondral bone. In the rheumatoid-factor-positive subtype, autoantibodies against the Fc portion of immunoglobulin G and citrullinated proteins mark a more destructive, adult-type rheumatoid process, whereas the seronegative subtype represents a more biologically diverse group with variable outcomes.
additionalDifferentials: Systemic lupus erythematosus and mixed connective tissue disease
Other JIA subtypes including systemic and psoriatic disease
additionalInvestigations: Rheumatoid factor and anti-citrullinated peptide antibodies to subclassify and gauge prognosis
Antinuclear antibody to inform uveitis risk
Inflammatory markers (erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein)
Radiographs, ultrasound or MRI of affected joints to detect synovitis and erosions
MRI of the temporomandibular joints when jaw involvement is suspected
Full blood count and film to help exclude malignancy and monitor therapy
Slit-lamp ophthalmology assessment as part of surveillance
redFlags: Rapidly progressive erosive disease with functional decline
Temporomandibular or cervical spine involvement threatening feeding or airway
Constitutional symptoms, night pain or cytopenias suggesting malignancy
Silent uveitis complications on ophthalmic review
reference.prognosis: The rheumatoid-factor-positive subtype tends to run a persistent, erosive course requiring sustained immunosuppression, whereas seronegative disease has a more variable outlook. Early aggressive treatment improves the likelihood of remission and reduces long-term joint damage and disability.
pitfalls: Underestimating disease severity because inflammatory markers can be only modestly raised
Missing temporomandibular joint disease, which is often clinically silent yet causes growth impairment
Delaying disease-modifying therapy and allowing irreversible erosions
Overlooking uveitis surveillance in antinuclear-antibody-positive children
Confusing an evolving connective tissue disease with seronegative polyarthritis
references: ILAR classification of juvenile idiopathic arthritis
ACR/PRINTO treatment recommendations for polyarticular JIA
management: Early aggressive disease-modifying therapy with methotrexate as first-line, aiming for remission and prevention of erosions
Escalate to biologic disease-modifying drugs such as tumour necrosis factor inhibitors for inadequate response, especially in rheumatoid-factor-positive erosive disease
Intra-articular and short courses of corticosteroids for flares, minimising long-term systemic steroid exposure
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for symptomatic relief of pain and stiffness
Regular slit-lamp screening for chronic anterior uveitis, particularly in antinuclear-antibody-positive children
Physiotherapy and occupational therapy, with attention to temporomandibular and cervical spine involvement affecting jaw growth, feeding and the airway
Monitor growth, bone health and drug toxicity, and support transition to adult services
Multidisciplinary paediatric rheumatology care with ophthalmology, orthodontic and dental input
